overlap.title: War on Moab: “fell every good tree”, or “thou shalt not destroy the trees”?
overlap.summary: Deuteronomy forbids destroying a besieged city’s food trees. In 2 Kings Elisha, speaking in the Lord’s name, tells Israel to fell every good tree in Moab, and they do.
overlap.reasoning: The law allows only trees that are not for food to be cut down in a siege. Elisha’s word, which opens “Thus saith the Lord”, tells the army attacking Moab’s cities to fell every good tree, with no exception, and verse 25 reports that they felled all the good trees. Because the act is commanded in the story, this is recorded as a contrast between two commands and not as a law broken.
overlap.scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV matches the Hebrew in both passages, and no V is claimed. The Hebrew verbs differ in the two passages (“destroy” and “cut down” in Deuteronomy, “fell” in Kings); the comparison rests on the act, not on a shared word. Deuteronomy speaks of the trees of a city under a long siege; Kings does not say whether the “good” trees of Moab were food trees or stood by besieged cities, and if they were neither, the two commands do not meet. Kings does not mention the law. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

overlap.title: A written law is entrusted for custody and periodic public reading
overlap.summary: The narrative attributes law writing to Moses and directs custody beside the ark and a seven-year public reading.
overlap.reasoning: A narrative attribution to Moses is evidence of the authorship claim made within the book, rather than external verification of the surviving book’s complete composition. The closing narrator’s perspective must be distinguished from the earlier law-writing attribution; this distinction alone does not identify an author, editor or date.
overlap.scope: This does not identify the deposited manuscript, establish its survival or show how regularly the reading occurred.

overlap.title: “Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God” — which words, and in which book?
overlap.summary: After the covenant at Shechem, Joshua is said to have written “these words in the book of the law of God”. The verse does not say which words he wrote, or whether the book is the book of the law that Moses wrote and had placed beside the ark, which the book of Joshua elsewhere calls “the book of the law of Moses”.
overlap.reasoning: Deuteronomy says Moses wrote the words of the law in a book “until they were finished” and had it put beside the ark. Joshua then writes in a book with a like name. If it is the same book, Joshua’s writing was added to that book after Moses, without establishing an addition to the substantive law; if it is another book, the passage speaks of a second writing that it does not describe. What “these words” covers — the covenant of that day, its statute and ordinance, or a longer account — is not said either, and it bears on what the passage claims about who wrote what.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that Joshua added a record of the Shechem covenant to the book Moses wrote; that “the book of the law of God” is a separate writing kept at the sanctuary; that “these words” are the statute and ordinance of verse 25 only; that the phrase points to the writing of the book of Joshua or of part of it. The record does not say that writing in the book would break any command. Brenton’s Greek as quoted has no article with “book” and has “laws” in the plural; that is noted and not examined. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV of Joshua for “book of the law” finds 1:8, 8:31, 8:34, 23:6 and 24:26, with “of Moses” at 8:31 and 23:6 and “of God” at 24:26 only; a search of the whole packaged KJV for “book of the law of God” finds Joshua 24:26 and Nehemiah 8:18, and Nehemiah 8:18 was not examined; Joshua 24:25–29 and Deuteronomy 31:24–26 were read in the KJV. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle which words Joshua wrote or in which book. A published record cites Deuteronomy 31:24–26 and Joshua 1:8 on the writing and keeping of the law, and another compares the place of the assembly in the Hebrew and the Greek; neither cites this question. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

overlap.title: “Michal took an image, and laid it in the bed” — what was it, and how did it come to be in David's house?
overlap.summary: To cover David’s escape Michal puts “an image” in his bed, and Saul’s messengers find it there. The Hebrew word is the one the KJV prints as “teraphim” in Judges, renders “images” where Rachel steals her father’s and Laban calls them “my gods”, and renders “idolatry” in Samuel’s rebuke of Saul. The verses compared do not say what the object was, whose it was, or what it was kept for.
overlap.reasoning: The object is the means of the escape, and the Hebrew gives it the definite article: “the teraphim”. The article alone does not establish its ownership or prior use in the household. In the other verses quoted the same Hebrew word names things a man calls “my gods” (Genesis 31:30), things made with an ephod for “an house of gods” (Judges 17:5), things Josiah put away with the idols (2 Kings 23:24), and the thing to which Samuel likens Saul’s stubbornness (1 Samuel 15:23). Here it lies in David’s bed, and the verses quoted pass no remark on it. What it was and whose it was decides whether the passage shows an object of worship kept in David’s house, something of Michal’s own, or a thing with another use.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that it was a household figure of the kind Laban calls his gods; that it belonged to Michal and not to David; that it was a figure kept for some use other than worship; that it was large enough to pass for a man in a bed. Limits: a shared Hebrew word does not show that the object in David’s house was the same kind of thing as Laban’s or Micah’s, or that it was used as theirs were; the Hebrew word is plural in form in every verse quoted, and the KJV renders it “an image” here and “images” in Genesis, so its form does not settle whether one object or several is meant; the verses quoted do not say the object had a human shape or size — they say it was laid in the bed and covered, and that Michal said “He is sick”; Rachel sits upon hers (Genesis 31:34), which says something of the size of those and nothing of this one; the passage does not say David knew of the object, and it records no word of blame or of approval; no finding of a broken law is proposed, because the verses quoted do not describe any act of worship. The KJV’s “an image” for the Hebrew “the teraphim”, the KJV’s “idolatry” at 15:23, and Brenton’s Greek word at 19:13 are stated here as wording and are not proposed as separate findings. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “teraphim” finds Judges 17:5, 18:14, 18:17, 18:18, 18:20 and Hosea 3:4 only, so the English word does not lead to this passage; the Hebrew word was confirmed by script in the Westminster Leningrad text of 1 Samuel 19:13, 19:16 and 15:23, Genesis 31:19 and 31:34, Judges 17:5 and 2 Kings 23:24, and the Hebrew Bible was not searched for its other occurrences; 1 Samuel 19:8–18 was read in the KJV. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the image was or whose it was. No H, G or V is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
